prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a party waives the right to compel arbitration by substantially utilizing the litigation machinery to the prejudice of the other party.

Cite at least six decisions of the Fourth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. [PLAINTIFF] WAIVED ANY RIGHT TO COMPEL ARBITRATION BY SUBSTANTIALLY UTILIZING THE LITIGATION MACHINERY.**

The right to arbitrate, like any contractual right, may be waived. *Am. Recovery Corp. v. Computerized Thermal Imaging, Inc.*, 96 F.3d 88, 95 (4th Cir. 1996). The Federal Arbitration Act's policy favoring arbitration does not excuse a party who invokes the judicial process and then seeks to abandon it. A party may not litigate in court and later retreat to arbitration when it suits its strategy. This Court has long held that a party waives arbitration when it so substantially utilizes the litigation machinery that compelling arbitration would be inconsistent with the right it now asserts. *Id.* at 95–96; *Patten Grading & Paving, Inc. v. Skanska USA Bldg., Inc.*, 380 F.3d 200, 204–05 (4th Cir. 2004); *Forrester v. Penn Lyon Homes, Inc.*, 553 F.3d 340, 343 (4th Cir. 2009).

**A. Prejudice is no longer required.**

This Court's earlier decisions often framed waiver as requiring prejudice to the opposing party. *See, e.g.*, *Rota-McLarty v. Santander Consumer USA, Inc.*, 700 F.3d 690, 700–01 (4th Cir. 2012); *Chorley Enters., Inc. v. Dickey's Barbecue Rests., Inc.*, 807 F.3d 553, 563–64 (4th Cir. 2015). The Supreme Court has since rejected that requirement. In *Morgan v. Sundance, Inc.*, 596 U.S. 411, 419 (2022), the Court held that federal courts may not create arbitration-specific waiver rules that demand a showing of prejudice. Waiver of the right to arbitrate is governed by the ordinary rule: waiver is the intentional relinquishment or abandonment of a known right, and the focus is on the waiving party's conduct, not on the effect on its opponent. *Id.* at 417–19. To the extent *Rota-McLarty*, *Chorley*, and similar decisions made prejudice a necessary element, they no longer control. The inquiry here is whether [Plaintiff] knowingly acted inconsistently with its right to arbitrate.

Even under the stricter pre-*Morgan* standard, [Plaintiff] would have waived arbitration. Prejudice only made the showing harder, so the same conduct that satisfies *Morgan* also satisfies the older cases.

**B. [Plaintiff]'s conduct was inconsistent with the right to arbitrate.**

This Court has looked to the totality of a party's litigation conduct, including the length of delay, the extent of the party's use of discovery and motion practice, and whether it sought merits rulings from the court. *See Patten Grading*, 380 F.3d at 204–05; *Am. Recovery*, 96 F.3d at 95–96; *see also Hightower v. GMRI, Inc.*, 272 F.3d 239, 242 (4th Cir. 2001). Each consideration points toward waiver here.

*First*, [Plaintiff] chose the judicial forum. It filed this action on [date], pleading [claims] that it now says are subject to arbitration. A plaintiff who files suit on arbitrable claims acts in a manner fundamentally at odds with an intent to arbitrate. *See Forrester*, 553 F.3d at 343.

*Second*, [Plaintiff] waited [number] months after filing, and [number] months after it knew of the arbitration clause, before raising arbitration. [Record cite.] During that time it [served/responded to written discovery, noticed or took depositions, negotiated a Rule 26(f) plan, and stipulated to a scheduling order]. [Record cite.]

*Third*, [Plaintiff] sought and obtained rulings on the merits. It [moved for a preliminary injunction / opposed Defendant's motion to dismiss / moved for partial summary judgment], and the district court [ruled]. [Record cite.] A party that invites the court to decide the merits and then seeks to start over before an arbitrator has made the very choice that waiver doctrine treats as binding. *See Am. Recovery*, 96 F.3d at 95–96.

*Fourth*, [Plaintiff] moved to compel only after [an adverse ruling / the close of discovery / Defendant's dispositive motion]. A motion made at that point looks like forum shopping, not the assertion of a right preserved all along.

Defendant also spent substantial resources litigating in the forum [Plaintiff] selected. Under *Morgan* that harm is not an element, but it confirms that [Plaintiff]'s conduct was inconsistent with any intent to arbitrate. On this record, [Plaintiff] intentionally relinquished its right to arbitrate. The district court's denial of the motion to compel should be affirmed.
